nodes.label: Hook JSON-in/JSON-out contract
nodes.rationale: smith writes one JSON object on stdin and reads one from stdout. Unknown fields are ignored so a hook written against a later version degrades instead of exploding.

nodes.label: PreToolUse hook
nodes.rationale: An allow decision means no objection, never let it through — a hook can only ever subtract authority.

nodes.label: PostToolUse hook
nodes.rationale: On failure it passes the result through with a warning: a post hook cannot un-write a file, and a model that believes its write failed retries it.

nodes.label: UserPromptSubmit hook
nodes.rationale: On failure it refuses the turn: the typical hook strips secrets, and 'send it anyway' leaks them to a third-party API where no later apology retrieves them.

nodes.label: Hooks are global-config only
nodes.rationale: Honouring a hook from a repository's own config would make `git clone && smith` a code-execution vector for whoever wrote the repository.

nodes.label: matcher is exact names, not a regex
nodes.rationale: A regex would be a dependency, a footgun, and a way for a typo to match nothing. A policy hook that silently applies to no tools is the single failure mode this feature must not have.

nodes.label: PreToolUse fails closed on timeout or garbage
nodes.source_location: ### What a timeout means differs per event
nodes.rationale: A gate that cannot answer has not consented. Failing open would leave the user believing a policy is enforced when it is not; failing closed is bounded and loud.

nodes.label: Hook output is untrusted data
nodes.rationale: A hook that shells out to a linter is quoting file contents back at smith, and the file may not be the user's. Every line is prefixed with '> ' so text faking the closing frame appears inside the quote.

nodes.label: The tool name is an input, never an output
nodes.rationale: A hook turning a read_file into a run_bash is either broken or hostile, and both deserve to stop the call rather than get a shrug.

nodes.label: Hooks run for subagents
nodes.rationale: A policy is authority the user granted and a child does not inherit it; a hook is authority the user withheld, and a child's calls are the least-watched in the system. The opposite default cannot be filtered back in, because a hook that never runs cannot ask to.

edges.source_location: hook text is treated exactly like tool output
an answer that cannot be read is not an answer
